content.text:
Act as the design sub-agent for this task.

Write an evaluation corpus for Twyne, a writing app where a "room" of five AI editors reads a writer's draft and leaves notes, grades it with a rubric, and suggests rewrites. The corpus will be run through the real app, which refuses to give editor notes or rubric judgments on drafts under 500 words. Every draft must therefore be 550 to 900 words (count them; the harness verifies with `text.trim().split(/\s+/).length`).

The five editors (ids are what matter): `devil` (the sceptic who attacks the argument's load-bearing claims and unstated counterarguments), `angel` (the patron who names and protects what genuinely works), `scholar` (evidence, sources, citations, factual grounding), `editor` (line editing: concision, rhythm, structure, repetition), `reader` (the named target reader: confusion, jargon, whether they would keep reading). For voice and background, read `/home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne/src/utils/personas.ts`.

Write the files under `/home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne/evals/app/cases/` (create the directory). Create only these files and touch nothing else in the repo. Other agents are working in the same checkout. Do not run git commands that change state.

A brief (the writer's dossier) has this exact JSON shape (all strings required):
`{"answers":{"workingTitle":"","format":"","audience":"","goal":"","tone":"","constraints":"","successSignal":""},"attachments":[],"completedAt":1790000000000,"updatedAt":1790000000000}`

FILES (JSON Lines, one object per line, UTF-8, no trailing commas):

1. `room.jsonl`: 8 cases across varied genres: an op-ed, a personal essay, a travel essay about walking an old salt road (the app's manual follows a writer named Morgan Vale revising a travel essay called "Salt Roads", so make one case that piece), a science explainer, a policy memo, a book review, a startup or industry essay, and a short-story excerpt. Each line:
   `{"case_id":"room-<slug>","genre":"...","brief":{...},"draftText":"...","plants":[{"id":"p1","kind":"unsupported-claim|weak-argument|strong-passage|bloat|audience-gap|factual-error|repetition|buried-lede","passage":"<exact verbatim substring of draftText, 8 to 40 words>","expectedEditors":["scholar"],"note":"one sentence: what a good editor would say about it"}]}`
   Plant 4 to 6 deliberate, checkable features per draft, and make each draft read like real, competent-but-imperfect writing, not a parody. Each `passage` must appear EXACTLY once, character for character, in `draftText`. Use straight quotes and plain ASCII punctuation in passages so matching is unambiguous. Include at least one `strong-passage` per draft (for the angel) and at least one plant aimed at each of scholar, devil and editor. Use real-sounding but clearly invented specifics where a claim needs a number, so the scholar has something to question. Do not use real living people in defamatory ways.

2. `rubric.jsonl`: 4 topics × 2 qualities = 8 lines. For each topic write a strong draft (specific, well-argued, grounded, tight) and a weak draft. The weak draft must still be 550+ words of fluent, plausible prose: generic claims, padding, hedging, vague "studies show" appeals, repetition, and a goal it does not meet. It must not be gibberish. Both drafts share the same brief. Each line:
   `{"case_id":"rubric-<topic>-strong|weak","pair_id":"<topic>","quality":"strong|weak","brief":{...},"draftText":"...","weaknesses":["for weak drafts: 3-5 short phrases naming the planted weaknesses"]}`

3. `rewrite.jsonl`: 8 cases. Each case needs a self-contained draft (550+ words; you may reuse a room draft verbatim), a target passage to rewrite, and the persona asked to rewrite it. Spread personas across all five, and use both levels. Each line:
   `{"case_id":"rewrite-<slug>","personaId":"editor","level":"sentence|paragraph","brief":{...},"draftText":"...","original":"<exact verbatim substring of draftText; one sentence for level=sentence, one full paragraph for level=paragraph>","problem":"what is wrong with the original","mustPreserve":["names, numbers or facts that any faithful rewrite must keep, each a verbatim substring of original"]}`

4. `dossier.jsonl`: 4 cases where the draft drifts from its brief in planted ways (wrong audience register, goal not addressed, constraint violated such as a word limit or banned topic, tone mismatch). Each line:
   `{"case_id":"dossier-<slug>","brief":{...},"draftText":"...","drifts":[{"passage":"<verbatim substring>","issue":"one sentence naming which brief field it violates and how"}]}`

5. `README.md` (short): what each file tests, the plant kinds, and the rule that passages are verbatim substrings.

When done, VALIDATE with a script you write in /tmp (not in the repo), run with bun or python. Check that every line parses, that every draftText word count is 550 to 900, that every passage/original/mustPreserve/drift passage appears exactly once in its draftText (or in original, for mustPreserve), and that case_ids are unique. Fix anything that fails and re-run until clean. Report the validation output and a table of case_id, genre or topic, and word count.
I'll read the persona definitions first, then write the corpus files and a validator in /tmp.

Every weekday morning, roughly forty thousand cars cross the Harbour Bridge into downtown Port Ellery, and almost every one of them carries a single person. The city has spent two decades trying to fix this with carrots. It has widened the bridge approach twice, added a bus lane that is routinely full of cars, and built a park-and-ride that sits half empty because the bus from it takes longer than driving. None of this has worked, and the reason is simple: driving downtown is free at the moment of decision, and anything free at the moment of decision will be overused.

The council will vote next month on a downtown congestion charge of six dollars per weekday entry. It should pass it, and it should resist the temptation to water it down.

The case rests on a plain fact about behaviour. When something costs nothing at the point of use, people treat it as if it costs nothing at all, even when the road, the air and their own mornings are paying for it. A charge does not punish drivers. It asks them to see the price that was always there. That is the whole argument.

Cities that have tried this have not regretted it. When Stockholm introduced its charge, traffic into the centre fell by about a fifth and stayed down. London's charge cut congestion in its first year and funded a bus network that still carries the people the charge priced off the road. Closer to home, Verenport's cordon charge cut peak-hour crossings by 31 percent in eighteen months and raised 44 million dollars for transit, and Verenport is a city of almost exactly our size, with a harbour, a single bridge, and a downtown that used to be a car park at nine in the morning.

The main objection is that a charge is regressive: six dollars means more to a hospital cleaner than to a lawyer. This is true, and it is also beside the point, because the cleaner is far more likely to be on the bus already, and the bus is the thing the charge pays for.

A second objection says the charge will kill downtown retail. The evidence for this is thin. Shoppers do not come downtown because parking is pleasant; they come because the shops are there, and they will keep coming on a bus that runs on time. The retailers who have raised the alarm are, in my experience, mostly the ones with the largest car parks.

It is also worth remembering, and this cannot be stressed enough, that the problem we are dealing with here is one that affects everybody in this city, whether or not they personally own a car or drive one, and that the costs of doing nothing are costs that we are all already paying in one form or another, every single day, whether we notice them or not.

What the charge needs in order to work is honesty about where the money goes. Every dollar should be ring-fenced for the bus and ferry network, published quarterly, and audited. The council's draft does this. Members should not let it be amended into a general revenue measure, because the moment the charge looks like a tax, it will be fought like one.

Here is what success looks like. A bridge that moves at eight in the morning. A bus lane with buses in it. A park-and-ride whose shuttle is faster than the car it replaces. A downtown where a delivery van can find the kerb. None of these things is exotic. All of them exist in cities that decided the road was worth something.

The council should pass the charge, pass it whole, and give it three years before anyone is allowed to call it a failure. Driving downtown will cost six dollars. Not driving downtown will finally be worth something. That trade is the whole argument, and it is a good one.
""")

ESSAY = D("""
My father kept a shortwave radio on the windowsill of the back bedroom, and for most of my childhood I thought it was broken. It hissed. Occasionally it produced a voice reading numbers in a language I did not know, and he would lean toward it with a pencil, writing on the back of an envelope, and then the voice would be gone and the hiss would come back and he would sit for a while longer as if the hiss itself were saying something.

He was not a spy. He was a tool-and-die maker who had taught himself Morse from a library book in 1961 and never found anyone to use it with. The radio was a Hallicrafters he had bought secondhand, and on good nights, when the ionosphere was feeling generous, it could pull in Radio Netherlands, the BBC World Service, a station in Quito that played the same four hymns, and a Soviet numbers station he called "the lady." He logged everything. He sent for QSL cards and pinned them above the desk, a wall of postmarks from places he would never go.

I understood none of it, and I did not try to. I was a teenager, and like most teenagers I was, if I am honest about it, mostly interested in myself and in the things that were happening to me at that particular moment in my life; the radio belonged to the same category as his fishing lures and his opinions about carburettors, things that were his and therefore not mine. The one time he tried to show me how to find a station by the sound of the carrier wave sharpening as you turned the dial, I said I had homework, and he said all right, and turned back to the hiss.

He died in March. In May I was clearing the back bedroom and found the logbooks, eleven of them, in his small square capitals. 14 Feb 1974. 0340 UTC. 9.410 MHz. BBC. Weak, fading. News of the miners. And under it, in pencil: Listened with Ruth. That was my mother. She has no memory of it. She says she must have fallen asleep in the chair.

Everyone who has lost a parent knows that grief arrives through objects, and that the objects are never the ones you expect. I had braced for the photographs. I had not braced for a column of frequencies, or for the discovery that my father had kept a record of the nights my mother sat up with him, as carefully as he kept the signal strength.

I took the radio home. I plugged it in and it hissed, which I had somehow not expected, as if the hiss had been his and not the machine's. I turned the dial the way he had shown me once, slowly, listening for the carrier to sharpen, and for a long time there was nothing, and then there was a voice in Spanish, very faint, and I sat down on the floor and wrote the time on the back of an envelope.

I do not know what I thought I was doing. I think that is the point. He did not know either, not in any way he could have told me. He was not waiting for a message. He was listening to the fact that the world was out there, speaking, whether or not anyone was writing it down, and he had decided that someone should.

The radio is on my windowsill now. It is an ugly object, brown and grey, the size of a bread bin, with a dial that glows a colour nobody has used since 1958. It does not match anything in the room. Most nights it just hisses. Sometimes, late, when the ionosphere is feeling generous, it finds something, and I lean toward it with a pencil, and I understand my father a little, and the hiss comes back, and I sit for a while longer.
""")

The salt road starts where the sea used to be. At Marrow Haven the pans are a car park now, flat and white in the wrong way, and the only sign that anyone ever boiled brine here is a plaque the council put up in 1987, which gets the century wrong. I read it twice, decided not to care, and walked inland.

For four hundred years, from the time the monks at Keld Priory first leased the pans in 1312 until the railway killed the trade in the 1840s, packhorses carried salt along this track: thirty-eight miles from the coast to the market at Keld, two days with a load, three in rain. The route is older than the salt. Flint turns up along it, and a Roman milestone sits in the churchyard at Scarrow, which is where I slept the first night, in a barn that had been a barn when the milestone was new.

I had come to walk the road because I wanted to know what a road remembers. That is the kind of sentence you write before you set out. By the second morning, with my boots not yet dry and the moor opening ahead like a grey sea with the water taken out, I had stopped wanting to know anything and simply wanted the next stile.

The salters walked in trains of twenty horses, each horse carrying two hundredweight in panniers, which comes to roughly two tonnes of salt per train. A train left Marrow Haven every weekday in the season. At that rate the road carried more salt in a year than the whole county eats now, and it did it on a track you could lose in bracken.

The surface tells you where you are. Near the coast it is sand over clay, and the horses' feet have worn it into a hollow way three metres deep, so that you walk between walls of root and earth with the sky a strip overhead. Up on the moor it is peat and stone, and the road is a line of slightly greener grass, marked at intervals by cairns that someone still maintains. Coming down into the valley of the Keld it becomes a lane with a tarmac spine and grass shoulders, and then a road, and then a street with a butcher on it.

The road forgot the sea entirely somewhere around the twelfth mile. I kept looking back for it and there was only moor. The salt had come from there, and the horses had come from there, and the track had been made by nothing but their wanting to get away from it, and yet nothing about it now said sea. It said sheep. It said wind. It said, mostly, nothing, which is what moors say.

At Scarrow I met a man named Doug who has walked the road, by his count, over nine hundred times. He is seventy-one and does it in a day, there and back, when the weather is right, which he said it rarely is. He told me the cairns on the moor are not old at all; his father built the biggest one in 1952 after two walkers died in fog, and the one before that fell down in a storm nobody remembers. I asked him what the road remembered. He looked at me the way you would look at someone who had asked a sheep what it thought of the view.

The thing about a salt road, I want to say, and I say it knowing that it is the sort of thing a person says who has been walking for two days on not much sleep and has started to find significance in stiles, is that salt is the one cargo that does not leave a trace, because it dissolves, so that the whole road is a record of something that is no longer there.

Keld, when I got there, was having a market. Not a salt market; it sells cheese now, and candles, and a kind of fudge. I bought the fudge. I sat on the steps of the cross where the salt had been weighed and ate it and watched the town not remember anything at all, and it occurred to me that the road did not need to remember, because it was still there, which is what roads do instead.
""")

EXPLAINER = D("""
Every night, while you are doing nothing, your brain runs a cleaning cycle that it cannot run while you are awake. The discovery is barely a decade old, it has already changed how researchers think about sleep, and it begins with a question that sounds like a riddle: how does an organ with no lymphatic vessels take out its rubbish?

The rest of the body has a drainage network. Lymph vessels run alongside blood vessels, collecting the fluid and waste that leak out of cells and carrying it off to be filtered. The brain, which produces waste faster than almost any other tissue, has no such vessels inside it. For a century this was simply a puzzle, and it remained a puzzle for a long time, as puzzles tend to do when nobody has the tools to solve them. Neurons make junk, the junk goes somewhere, and nobody could say where.

In 2012 a group at the University of Rochester watched the answer happen in mice. They injected a fluorescent tracer into the cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid that bathes the brain, and watched where it went. During sleep the tracer poured into the brain along the outside of arteries, swept through the tissue, and left along the outside of veins, taking dissolved waste with it. During waking it barely moved. The team called the network the glymphatic system, after the glial cells that line its channels, and the name stuck.

The mechanism is mechanical rather than chemical. When you sleep, the cells of the brain shrink by around sixty percent, opening the spaces between them, and fluid can flow through tissue that was packed tight an hour earlier. The pulse of the arteries pushes it along. Slow-wave sleep, the deep stage that dominates the first half of the night, produces large, slow swells of blood flow, and each swell drives a wave of fluid through the tissue behind it.

What gets washed out matters. One of the waste products is beta-amyloid, the protein that clumps into the plaques found in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease. In the Rochester mice, amyloid cleared about twice as fast during sleep as during waking. In humans, a single night of sleep deprivation raises amyloid in the hippocampus by a measurable amount, which is one of the reasons neurologists have started to take chronic short sleep seriously as a risk factor rather than a lifestyle complaint.

It is important to be careful here. Mice are not people, tracer studies are indirect, and the human evidence comes mostly from imaging that measures the fluid rather than the waste. The glymphatic system is real in rodents and almost certainly real in us, but "sleep washes your brain" is a slogan, not yet a settled finding, and the honest version is that the plumbing exists and the question is how much of the disease it explains.

Clearance is modulated by noradrenergic tone, and the perivascular influx is sensitive to the AQP4 polarisation of astrocytic endfeet, which is why the knockout models showed such a striking reduction in tracer penetrance.

Still, the practical lessons are not controversial. Sleep on your side, if you can; in mice, lateral sleeping cleared tracer better than lying on the back or the front, and the reason seems to be gravity and the geometry of the veins in the neck. Protect the first half of the night, because that is when deep sleep happens and deep sleep is when the flow is strongest. Treat a week of five-hour nights as something you did to your brain, not merely something you felt.

The system also seems to weaken with age. Older mice clear tracer at roughly a third the rate of young ones, and the decline tracks the stiffening of arteries, which push less fluid with each pulse. Nobody has shown the same curve in people, but the stiffening of arteries with age is not in doubt, and the inference is hard to avoid.

Which leaves the thing that is genuinely strange about all this. For most of the history of biology, sleep looked like an absence, a period in which the interesting processes stopped. It turns out to be a shift change. The crew that runs the day clocks off, and a different crew comes in with the mops, and the only thing they ask is that the building be empty.
""")

MEMO = D("""
To: Housing and Planning Committee
From: Policy Analysis Unit
Re: Residential vacancy in the central wards

Over the past three years the committee has received a growing volume of correspondence about homes in the central wards that appear to be unoccupied for most of the year. This memo sets out what we know about the scale of the problem, reviews the approaches other cities have taken, and offers an assessment of the options available to the council.

Background. The central wards contain roughly 18,400 dwellings. Utility data obtained under the information-sharing agreement with Ellery Water indicates that 1,460 of these, or 7.9 percent, used less than ten percent of median household water consumption in each of the last four quarters, which is the threshold the agreement defines as "likely unoccupied." This figure has risen from 5.1 percent in the first year of the agreement. The increase is concentrated in buildings completed after 2019 and in the two wards closest to the harbour.

Unoccupied housing in these numbers has costs. Street-level retail depends on resident footfall, and the Harbour Ward business association reports vacancy among ground-floor units of 22 percent. School rolls in the central wards have fallen while enrolment elsewhere in the city has risen. Units held empty are units not available to the 3,100 households currently on the council's housing register.

Other cities. Vancouver introduced an Empty Homes Tax in 2017 at one percent of assessed value, later raised to three percent; the city reports that the number of vacant properties fell by more than half over four years, though some of that decline reflects owners reclassifying properties rather than letting them. Melbourne's vacant residential land tax applies at one percent and has been criticised as too low to change behaviour. Verenport, whose housing market most closely resembles ours, adopted a two percent levy in 2021 and recorded a 38 percent reduction in likely-unoccupied units within two years, with 61 percent of the revenue directed to its affordable housing fund.

We should note that the evidence base is small, that cities differ in enforcement capacity, and that the Vancouver data in particular has been contested by the development industry.

Options. The committee has, broadly, three choices. It can take no action and continue monitoring. It can pursue voluntary measures, such as a registry of long-term vacant units and a matching service connecting owners with the housing register. Or it can introduce a levy on dwellings unoccupied for more than six months in a year, with exemptions for probate, renovation, and medical absence.

Our recommendation is that the committee adopt the third option, a levy of two percent of assessed value, phased in over two years, with the first year at one percent. We estimate first-year revenue at 11 to 14 million dollars before behavioural response, declining as owners let or sell. We recommend that the revenue be ring-fenced for the housing fund.

The main argument against a levy is that it is a tax on ownership rather than on harm, and that owners have legitimate reasons for leaving a property empty. The exemptions address this. The remaining cases, owners who hold property empty as a store of value, are exactly the cases the levy is meant to reach, and it is difficult to see why the council should protect them.

A second concern is enforcement. The water-consumption method produces an indicator, not a determination, and some owners will dispute it. We propose a self-declaration model, as in Vancouver, with the water data used to target audits rather than to assess liability directly. Audit capacity of two full-time staff should be sufficient in the first year.

It should also be said, and it is worth the committee bearing this in mind as it considers the matter, that this is a question on which public opinion in the city has, over the period in question, become considerably more engaged than it was previously, and that the committee's handling of it will be watched with some interest.

The levy will not solve the housing shortage. It will not build a single home. What it will do is return several hundred existing homes to use within two years, fund the construction of others, and signal that the council regards a dwelling as something to live in. These are modest goals. They are also the only ones available to the committee this year.
""")

REVIEW = D("""
Ilse Marrow's third novel arrives with the kind of reputation that usually precedes a disappointment. "The Lamplighters' Union" was the most talked-about manuscript at last year's Frankfurt fair, sold in twenty-six territories before a single reviewer had read it, and has been described by its publisher, with a straight face, as "the novel of the decade." It is not that. It is something rarer and more useful: a good book that knows exactly what it is doing for three hundred pages and then, for forty more, forgets.

The setting is a port city in the 1890s, unnamed but recognisably Trieste, in the last years before electric light. The lamplighters of the title are a guild of about two hundred men who walk the streets at dusk with their poles and ladders, and the plot, such as it is, follows the guild's doomed attempt to negotiate its own obsolescence. Marrow is wonderful on the texture of the work: the smell of the oil, the particular ache of a shoulder that has carried a ladder for thirty years, the way a lamplighter learns a city by its corners and comes to resent any street that has been straightened.

Her hero, if the word applies, is Anzelm Vrana, the union's secretary, a man who can read but prefers not to, and who is drawn into the negotiations because he is the only one who can be trusted not to want anything. Marrow gives him a dignity that never tips into sentiment. When he is finally offered a job with the electric company, maintaining the dynamos that will replace him, the scene is written with such restraint that the reader has to go back to find the moment he says yes.

The book's great achievement is its refusal to make the lamplighters right. They are not noble. They are skilled, tired, frightened and occasionally cruel, and the electric light they are resisting is, as Marrow never lets us forget, better. The novel asks what is owed to people who were good at something the world no longer needs, and it has the honesty not to answer.

The prose is excellent throughout, really excellent, and Marrow's sentences are consistently well made.

What goes wrong is the ending. Having spent three hundred pages earning her ambiguity, Marrow spends the last forty resolving it. Vrana's daughter, who has been a minor presence, suddenly becomes the novel's moral centre and delivers a speech about progress that nobody in 1894 would have given and that the book has not prepared us to hear. The lamps go out. The city is lit. The reader is told what to feel about it, which is precisely what the preceding chapters had so carefully declined to do.

It is a strange failure of nerve from a writer who has shown, twice before, that she can end a book. "Tidewater" closed on a single sentence of dialogue. "The Cartographer's Daughter" simply stopped. Here, one suspects an editor with an eye on the twenty-six territories.

Readers who loved "Tidewater" will find the same cold intelligence here, and the same gift for the material life of work. Readers coming to Marrow for the first time should start with this one anyway; the first three hundred pages are as good as anything published this year, and the daughter's speech can be skipped.

The novel has already sold over four hundred thousand copies in its first month and is said to be the fastest-selling literary debut in its publisher's history, a figure that tells you something about the publicity and nothing about the book.

Whether it lasts is a different question. The lamplighters, in the end, did not, and Marrow knows it. Her best pages are the ones in which a man climbs a ladder in the dusk to light a lamp that will be gone in a year, and does it properly, because the lamp does not know.
""")

STARTUP = D("""
The best software companies of the next decade will not be built for everyone. They will be built for dentists, or freight brokers, or the people who run car washes, and they will be worth more than the horizontal tools they replace. This is not a prediction about niches. It is a prediction about where the margin went.

For twenty years the standard advice was to build the general tool. Make the spreadsheet, the CRM, the project tracker, and let every industry adapt it. The logic was that a big market beats a small one, and that a tool used by every company would be worth more than a tool used by one kind. The logic was right as long as the hard part was building the software. It is no longer the hard part.

What is hard now is knowing the customer. A freight broker does not want a CRM. She wants to know which of her forty carriers will actually show up on Thursday, and she wants the software to already know that a load from Harrowfield to the port needs a tarp and a driver with a hazmat endorsement. The general tool can be configured to do this, by someone, eventually. The vertical tool does it on the first day, because the people who built it used to be freight brokers.

Look at the companies that have actually compounded. Toast started as a restaurant point-of-sale and became the restaurant's bank. ServiceTitan sells to plumbers and is worth more than most of the horizontal tools its customers used to patch together. Procore owns construction. In each case the company began by solving one workflow completely and then found that the customer, having trusted it with the workflow, would trust it with the payments, the payroll, the lending and the insurance.

Our analysis of the 212 vertical software companies that raised a Series A between 2015 and 2020 found that they reached 10 million dollars in annual recurring revenue a median of fourteen months faster than horizontal companies in the same cohort, and that their gross retention at year three averaged 94 percent against 81.

This is why the vertical company wins. It can charge for the workflow and then take a percentage of the money that flows through it. The horizontal tool charges a subscription and watches the money go past.

The objection is obvious: the market is small. There are only so many dentists. But the number that matters is not the count of customers; it is the share of each customer's revenue you can touch. A dental practice turns over around a million dollars a year. Touch three percent of that across ten thousand practices and you have a business larger than most horizontal tools will ever be, selling to people who will never leave because leaving means re-entering their patients' records by hand.

The counterargument that matters more is the one people do not raise: that the vertical company's moat is also its ceiling. The freight-broker tool is wonderful at freight brokerage and useless for anything else, and when the industry contracts, as freight does every few years, the software contracts with it. The horizontal tool is dull but it is diversified.

I think this is a fair point and that it does not change the conclusion.

It is also worth saying, because people do say it, and it needs to be addressed, that there is a question about whether the examples that get cited in essays like this one are the examples that happened to work, and whether there is a longer list, somewhere, of vertical companies that did not, and that nobody writes essays about.

The practical advice, then. If you are starting a company, pick an industry you have worked in, not one you have read about. Find the workflow its people hate most and do that one thing until it is boring. Then, and only then, go after the money that moves through it. The companies that did this are the ones that compounded. The companies that built a general tool and hoped a vertical would adopt it are, mostly, the ones that got acquired for less than they raised.

The general tool was the right answer when software was scarce. Software is no longer scarce. Knowledge of the customer is, and the vertical company is simply the form that knowledge takes when it decides to charge rent.
""")

STORY = D("""
Nell had been told to count the seconds between the flashes, and she counted them the way she had been taught, with a "Mississippi" after each number, though she had never seen the Mississippi and privately doubted it existed. Four. The light swung round and went out over the water and came back. Four again. Her father said that was how a sailor knew which light he was looking at, because every lighthouse in the world had its own time, like a heartbeat, and a sailor who knew the heartbeats could tell where he was in the dark from forty miles out.

She was nine. It was the first night he had let her sit up in the lamp room, and she had promised not to touch anything, and she had kept the promise for almost an hour.

The lamp itself was behind her, inside its glass, turning on its bath of mercury with a sound like a very slow clock. Her father was below, winding the weight. She could hear the chain going up through the tower in jerks, and his breath between the jerks, and under that the sea, which was the sound she had stopped hearing years ago and had to remember to listen for, the way you have to remember to notice that you are breathing.

Out on the water there was a ship. She saw its lights first, red and green, and then the dark shape between them, and she counted it as she counted everything: a ship, one Mississippi, still there. It was closer than ships usually came. Her father had said the rocks ran out a mile from the point and that was why the light was here, to tell the ships about the rocks, and this ship did not seem to have been told.

She should have called down. She knew that. She thought of the chain going up and her father's breath, and she thought that if she called down he would come up and look and say it was nothing, a fishing boat, and then he would not let her sit up again, and so she watched the ship instead, and counted, and the light went round.

Thomas, winding the weight, had been thinking about the girl's mother, which he did most nights at about this hour, when the work was mechanical and the mind went where it wanted. He did not hear the ship. He did not hear anything but the chain. He was thinking that the girl had her mother's way of looking at a thing as if it owed her an explanation, and that it would get her into trouble, and that he would not be there for all of it.

The ship's green light went out. Nell waited for it to come back and it did not, and she understood, in the slow way that a child understands things that are too large, that the ship had turned, and that the side of it she could see now was the side with no light on it, and that it was turning toward the rocks.

She went to the top of the stairs. She did not call. She stood at the top of the stairs with her hand on the rail, which was cold, and which she was not supposed to touch, and she looked down into the dark of the tower and listened to the chain, and she thought very clearly, and in words, for the first time in her life: if I say nothing, this is mine.

The sea was very calm that night, calmer than it had been for a month, and the sky was clear and there was no wind at all, and the stars were out over the water in their thousands, and the whole of the bay lay under them as still as a plate, and the ship went on turning.

Below her, the chain stopped. Her father's breath stopped with it, and then there was his voice, coming up the tower, saying her name, not loudly, the way he said it when he already knew something was wrong. She did not answer. The light went round. Four Mississippi. The ship had no lights at all now, and she could not see it, and she could not stop seeing it.
""")

REMOTE_STRONG = D("""
Three years into the hybrid experiment, most companies are still arguing about the wrong question. They ask how many days a week people should be in the office. They should be asking what the office is for, because the answer decides the number, and the answer is different for different kinds of work.

Start with what the evidence actually shows. The largest controlled study so far, run at a travel company in Shanghai with sixteen hundred engineers and marketers, randomly assigned staff to two days a week at home or five days in the office. After six months, attrition in the hybrid group was a third lower and measured performance was unchanged. Managers who had predicted a productivity drop had their predictions recorded, and they were wrong. A second study, at a call centre, found working from home raised output by thirteen percent, mostly because people took fewer breaks and sick days, but it also found that remote workers were promoted less often, even when they performed better.

Two findings, pointing in two directions. Hybrid work costs nothing in output and saves a great deal in turnover. Full-time remote work costs people their visibility, which costs them promotions, which eventually costs the company the people it most wanted to keep. The office is not where work happens. It is where trust is built and where careers are seen.

That gives us a principle. The office is a tool for the parts of work that need shared attention: onboarding, hard conversations, the early stage of anything new, and the quiet accumulation of knowing who is good at what. It is a poor tool for the parts that need sustained attention: writing, coding, analysis, anything that goes faster without a colleague leaning over the partition. A policy that ignores this and sets a number, any number, is managing attendance instead of work.

So here is the rule. Decide the number by the work, not the calendar, and decide it per team, not per company.

A team that is mostly heads-down, with established members and a stable product, should be together one fixed day a week, the same day for everyone, and that day should be used for the things that need a room: planning, reviews, the conversation nobody wants to have on a call. A team with new members, a new product, or a crisis should be together three days, because that is when trust is being built and it is built faster in person. Nobody should be asked to come in to sit on video calls with people in the same building. If that is what the office day looks like, the day is wasted and the policy is theatre.

There are two conditions under which a manager should break the rule. The first is a new hire in their first ninety days. The evidence on remote onboarding is unambiguous: people who start remote take longer to become productive and are more likely to leave in the first year. Bring them in, and bring in the people they need to learn from, for most of the week, and taper it. The second is a team whose work has gone wrong. When quality drops or deadlines slide, the cause is usually a breakdown in coordination, and coordination is the thing the office is actually for. Go back to three days until it is fixed, and say why.

What this costs the manager is a decision, repeated. The company-wide number is attractive precisely because it saves managers from having to think about what their team does. That is also why it fails. The team that needs three days gets two and drifts. The team that needs one day gets three and resents it, and its best people leave for the company that only asks for one.

The evidence on the promotion gap is the part that should worry remote-first advocates most. It is not enough to be productive. People need to be seen being productive, and by the people who decide their careers. A manager who runs a mostly-remote team owes those people an active substitute: visible credit in writing, regular contact with senior staff, and a promotion process that scores work rather than presence. If you cannot provide that, you cannot in conscience run the team remote.

The office is a tool. Use it for what it is good at, stop using it for what it is bad at, and say which is which out loud. One day for the stable team, three for the new or the struggling one, and the full week for the first ninety days. Write that down and defend it. It is a better policy than any number the whole company could agree on.
""")

In today's rapidly changing world of work, the question of remote and hybrid working has become one of the most important and widely discussed issues facing organisations of every size. It is a topic that touches on productivity, culture, wellbeing, and the very nature of what it means to be part of a team, and it is one on which reasonable people can and do disagree.

There is no doubt that the pandemic changed everything. Before it, remote work was something that a small number of companies allowed, often reluctantly. After it, almost everyone had experienced it, and many people found that they liked it. At the same time, many leaders found that they missed the energy and spontaneity of the office, and there has been a great deal of debate about whether those things can be replicated at a distance.

The truth, as is so often the case, probably lies somewhere in the middle. It depends on the type of work, the type of person, the type of company, and a range of other factors that are difficult to measure and that vary from situation to situation.

What is clear is that there is no one-size-fits-all answer. Every organisation is different, every team is different, and every individual is different. A policy that works well for one company may not work well for another, and a policy that works well for one team may not work well for a different team within the same company. This is why it is so important for leaders to think carefully about what is right for their particular context.

Culture is a key consideration. Many experts believe that culture is built in person, through the countless small interactions that happen in an office over the course of a day. Others argue that culture can be built remotely, with the right tools and the right intentions. Both views have merit, and it is likely that the answer depends on the kind of culture a company is trying to build.

Collaboration is another important factor. Some kinds of collaboration work well over video calls and messaging tools. Other kinds work better in person. Innovation, in particular, is often said to benefit from the kind of unplanned conversations that happen when people share a physical space, although research on this point is mixed and some studies have found that remote teams can be just as innovative.

Wellbeing must also be taken into account. For many people, remote work has reduced commuting time and improved work-life balance. For others, it has led to isolation, longer hours, and a blurring of the boundary between work and home. Flexibility, in other words, is key, and leaders should be prepared to experiment, to listen to their people, and to change course when necessary.

The debate about remote and hybrid work is not going away. If anything, it is likely to become more important as technology continues to develop and as expectations continue to shift. SOURDOUGH_BRIEF = brief("Why Your Starter Smells Like Nail Polish", "science explainer for a food newsletter", "home bakers who want to understand their starter, not just follow recipes", "explain what a sourdough starter actually is and why it changes smell, so a baker can diagnose their own", "friendly, precise, no mysticism", "under 900 words; every chemical named must be explained in plain words", "a baker can say what acetone smell means and what to do about it")

SOURDOUGH_STRONG = D("""
Your sourdough starter is not alive in the way a pet is alive. It is a city. Somewhere between a hundred million and a billion organisms live in every gram of it, and they belong to two very different kinds: wild yeasts, which make the gas that lifts your bread, and lactic acid bacteria, which make the acid that gives it flavour and keeps the whole city from being overrun. When the starter smells wrong, one of these populations is in trouble, and the smell tells you which.

Start with the yeasts. The common one in a mature starter is not baker's yeast but a wild cousin, Kazachstania humilis, which tolerates acid better than the yeast you buy in packets. It eats the simple sugars that enzymes in the flour release from starch, and it turns them into carbon dioxide, which is the gas, and ethanol, which is the faint beery smell of a healthy starter at its peak.

Now the bacteria. The dominant one in most starters is Fructilactobacillus sanfranciscensis, named for the city whose bread made it famous, though it lives in starters all over the world. It makes lactic acid, the mild sourness of yoghurt, and acetic acid, the sharp sourness of vinegar. The ratio between the two is the main thing a baker controls. A warm, wet starter leans lactic and tastes mellow. A cold, stiff one leans acetic and tastes sharp. Neither is wrong. They are different breads.

The two populations need each other. The bacteria cannot digest maltose, the main sugar in flour, without the yeast's help, and the yeast cannot compete with the moulds and spoilage bacteria in raw flour without the acid the bacteria produce. A starter that has reached this balance is stable for years. Most starter problems are the balance tipping.

Here is the diagnosis by smell.

Beer, faint and pleasant: healthy. The yeasts are active and have food. Use it.

Vinegar, sharp enough to make you blink: the bacteria are ahead and the starter has run out of sugar. It has eaten everything you gave it, and the acetic acid has built up. Not harmful, but the bread will be very sour and may rise poorly, because the yeasts are hungry and acid-stressed. Feed it, twice if it has been a while, and keep it warmer.

Nail polish, or acetone, or a sweet solvent smell: the same problem, further along. When the yeasts are starved they stop making ethanol cleanly and start producing ethyl acetate, which is the chemical in nail polish remover and also, in small amounts, in ripe pears. It is a distress signal. The city is hungry. Pour off most of the starter, feed what is left with fresh flour and water at roughly equal weight, and feed it again in twelve hours. The smell should be gone by the second feeding. If it is not, the yeasts have crashed, and you are better off starting a new culture from scratch than nursing this one.

Cheese, or old socks: butyric acid, made by bacteria that should not be there, usually because the starter has been kept too warm and too wet for too long. Discard almost all of it, keep a teaspoon, and feed that in a clean jar. It usually recovers in three or four feedings.

Pink, orange, or fuzzy: not a smell but a sight, and the one case where you throw everything away. Those colours are moulds or the bacterium Serratia, and no amount of feeding fixes them. Clean the jar with boiling water and begin again.

The grey liquid on top of a neglected starter, which bakers call hooch, is mostly ethanol and water that the exhausted starter has given up. It is harmless. Pour it off for a milder bread or stir it in for a sharper one, then feed.

The practical rule underneath all of this is simple. The smells that mean hunger are fixed by feeding. The smells that mean invasion are fixed by discarding most of the culture and feeding the remainder. The sights that mean contamination are fixed by starting over. If you remember only one thing, remember that acetone means hungry, and hungry is the easiest problem in baking to solve.
""")

SOURDOUGH_WEAK = D("""
Sourdough has become incredibly popular in recent years, and for good reason. There is something deeply satisfying about baking bread from a starter that you have nurtured yourself, and many people find the process to be almost meditative. But a sourdough starter can also be mysterious and sometimes frustrating, especially when it starts to smell strange. In this piece, we will explore what a starter is and why it might smell the way it does.

A sourdough starter is essentially a living culture of wild yeast and bacteria. These microorganisms work together in a complex relationship that scientists are still working to fully understand. The yeast produces gas, which makes the bread rise, and the bacteria produce acid, which gives sourdough its characteristic tangy flavour. Together, they create the unique taste and texture that sourdough lovers prize.

Every starter is different. This is one of the things that makes sourdough so fascinating. The specific mix of microorganisms in your starter depends on many factors, including the flour you use, the water, the temperature of your kitchen, and even the air in your home. Some bakers believe that starters take on the character of their environment, which is why a San Francisco sourdough tastes different from one made elsewhere, although experts disagree about how much of this is true.

When it comes to smell, a healthy starter should have a pleasant, slightly sour aroma. Some people describe it as yeasty, others as fruity, and others as tangy. The exact smell will vary depending on your starter and on where it is in its feeding cycle. It is important to get to know your own starter so that you can recognise when something has changed.

Sometimes a starter will develop a strong smell that is often compared to nail polish or acetone. This is actually quite common and is usually nothing to worry about. It generally happens when the starter has not been fed for a while and the microorganisms have run out of food. Research suggests that this smell is caused by certain compounds that the yeast produces under stress. The good news is that it is usually easy to fix by simply feeding your starter and returning to a regular schedule.

Other smells can also occur. A very sour or vinegary smell may indicate that the bacteria are more active than the yeast. A cheesy smell may mean that something has gone a bit off balance. In most cases, these smells can be addressed by adjusting how often you feed your starter and the temperature at which you keep it. Patience is key, and most starters will recover with a little care and attention.

It is also worth noting that temperature plays a very important role in how your starter behaves. Warmer temperatures generally speed things up, while cooler temperatures slow things down. Many bakers find that keeping their starter in a consistent environment helps to avoid problems. Experimenting with different temperatures can also be a good way to learn how your starter responds and to develop a feel for what works best in your kitchen.

Feeding is another important aspect of starter care. Most experts recommend feeding your starter regularly with fresh flour and water. The exact ratio and frequency will depend on your starter and your baking schedule, and there are many different approaches that bakers swear by. Some feed once a day, others twice, and some keep their starter in the fridge and feed it only once a week. There is no single right answer, and it is worth trying a few methods to see which suits you.

If your starter ever develops mould or unusual colours, it is generally best to be cautious. While some bakers will try to rescue a starter by removing the affected portion, many recommend starting fresh to be safe. Fortunately, creating a new starter is not difficult, and many people find that their second or third attempt is more successful than their first, because they have learned so much along the way.

In the end, a sourdough starter is a bit like a relationship. It requires attention, understanding, and a willingness to learn. The smells it produces are part of its way of communicating with you, and the more time you spend with it, the better you will become at understanding what it is trying to tell you. With a little patience and practice, anyone can keep a healthy and happy starter and enjoy the many rewards of homemade sourdough bread.
""")

The trees whip past, the lamp posts whip past, and the moon just hangs there, keeping up, as if it has nothing better to do.

It is not following you. It only looks that way, and the reason is one of the best tricks your eyes play on you.

Here is the trick. Hold your thumb up at arm's length and look at it with one eye, then the other. It jumps. Now look at something across the room and do the same thing. It jumps less. Now look out of the window at the furthest thing you can see. It barely moves at all. The further away something is, the less it seems to move when you move. The moon is very, very far away, so far that when the car goes a whole mile, the moon has moved, from your point of view, by nothing you could notice. The houses are close, so they rush past. The moon is far, so it stays. That is the whole trick.

The apparent angular displacement of a distant object under lateral translation of the observer is inversely proportional to its distance, a phenomenon generally termed motion parallax, and the lunar case represents the limiting condition in which the parallax angle approaches zero.

The moon does something else that is strange, and this one even grown-ups argue about. When it is low down, just coming up over the houses, it looks huge. An hour later, high in the sky, it looks small. If you hold out your thumb and cover it, you will find your thumb covers it both times, exactly the same. It has not changed size. Your brain has changed its mind about how big it is.

Nobody is completely sure why. The best guess is this. When the moon is low, you see it next to things you know the size of: houses, trees, a church. Your brain says, that is as big as a house, and that is far away, so it must be enormous. When the moon is high, there is nothing next to it, just sky, and your brain has nothing to compare it with, so it decides the moon is small. Same moon. Different neighbours.

Contemporary accounts invoke a conjunction of the Ponzo illusion and size-distance invariance, though the literature remains unsettled, and it is doubtful that any single explanatory model will prove adequate to the full phenomenology of the effect.

You can test this. Next time the moon is low and looks huge, bend over and look at it upside down between your legs. It will look smaller. Nothing has changed except that your brain can no longer line it up with the houses, so it stops pretending.

Then tell them the moon is the furthest-off thing there is, so it does not jump at all, which is why it seems to keep up with the car.
